title: Brute force, by the numbers
summary: Key space, guesses per second and years: why 56 bits fell, why 128 bits will not, and why passwords are the weak spot.

steps.title: Counting keys
body: A key of *n* bits has **2ⁿ** possible values. Brute force tries them one by one and on average finds the right one after **half**: 2ⁿ⁻¹ guesses.
Every extra bit **doubles** the work. So 128 bits is not "a bit more than 64": it is 2⁶⁴ (about 18 billion billion) times more work.

Step through the loop to see what a trillion guesses a second achieves against different key sizes. That rate is generous; the whole Bitcoin network does about 10²¹ SHA-256 hashes a second, and even that does not dent 128 bits.

code: double perSecond = 1e12;            // a trillion guesses a second
double guesses = Math.Pow(2, bits - 1);   // on average, half the key space

steps.prompt: How many decimal digits does the number of 128-bit keys have? Estimate it with 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³ (1,024 ≈ 1,000): 2¹²⁸ = 2⁸ × 2¹²⁰.
steps.explain: 2¹²⁸ is about 3.4 × 10³⁸. For comparison, the universe is about 4 × 10¹⁷ seconds old.

steps.prompt: Is AES-256 "twice as strong" as AES-128?
options: No: it has 2¹²⁸ times more keys; both are far beyond brute force today, and 256 adds margin against future attacks such as quantum search
No, it is weaker because the key schedule is longer
steps.explain: Bits add exponentially. Nobody brute-forces AES-128; AES-256 is chosen for long-lived secrets and the quantum margin you will meet later in this module.

steps.title: Years to search a key space
prompt: Write `double YearsToSearch(int bits, double guessesPerSecond)`: the **average** time to find a key by brute force, `2^(bits - 1) / guessesPerSecond` seconds, converted to years with 31,557,600 seconds per year.
template: Dojo.Check("56 bits at a billion a second is about 1.14 years", Math.Abs(YearsToSearch(56, 1e9) - 1.1417) < 0.001, YearsToSearch(56, 1e9).ToString());
Dojo.Check("one extra bit doubles the time", Math.Abs(YearsToSearch(57, 1e9) / YearsToSearch(56, 1e9) - 2) < 1e-9, "not double");
Dojo.Check("128 bits at a trillion a second is over 10^18 years", YearsToSearch(128, 1e12) > 1e18, YearsToSearch(128, 1e12).ToString("E2"));
Dojo.Check("40 bits falls in seconds", YearsToSearch(40, 1e12) * 31_557_600 < 1, (YearsToSearch(40, 1e12) * 31_557_600).ToString());
hints: `Math.Pow(2, bits - 1)` is the average number of guesses.
Divide by the rate to get seconds, then by 31,557,600.

steps.prompt: Match each key size to its real-world status.
pairs: Broken in seconds on a laptop
Broken in a day by purpose-built hardware in 1998
Out of reach for most, but no longer recommended
Beyond brute force for any classical computer
steps.explain: The jump from "broken" to "impossible" happens over a few dozen bits.

steps.title: The weak spot is the human
body: Nobody guesses a random 128-bit key, so attackers guess what *people* choose instead. A password's strength is its **entropy**: for a truly random choice of `length` symbols from an alphabet of size `N`, that is `length × log₂(N)` bits.
| 12 random letters and digits (62 symbols) | about 71.5 bits |
| a human-chosen "P@ssw0rd!" | far less than its length suggests |

Under 40 bits falls to a GPU in minutes against a fast hash. That is why passwords go through slow KDFs (PBKDF2, Argon2: module 2 and the *Authentication & JWT* topic) and why keys are **derived** with a KDF, never typed in.

steps.explain: Each random lowercase letter adds log₂(26) ≈ 4.7 bits and each random alphanumeric character about 5.95. Doubling the length doubles the bits.

steps.title: How long must a random secret be?
prompt: - `int MinLength(double targetBits, int alphabetSize)`: the shortest length that reaches **at least** `targetBits` (round up).
solution: double EntropyBits(int length, int alphabetSize) => length * Math.Log2(alphabetSize);
int MinLength(double targetBits, int alphabetSize) => (int)Math.Ceiling(targetBits / Math.Log2(alphabetSize));
template: Dojo.Check("8 lowercase letters is about 37.6 bits", Math.Abs(EntropyBits(8, 26) - 37.6035) < 0.001, EntropyBits(8, 26).ToString());
Dojo.Eq("MinLength(80, 10) for a numeric code", 25, MinLength(80, 10));
